transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)

Attendees:
- Jordan Patel (Redwood AE)
- Maya Chen (Redwood SE)
- Ibrahim Ortiz (Redwood Support)
- Lee Park (CTO, Polaris Systems)
- Samira Noor (Lead ML Eng, Polaris)
- Ethan Ruiz (SRE, Polaris)
- Talia Gomez (PM, Polaris)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for carving time today. we wanted to focus in on the eviction waves you've been seeing, and go through a reproducible plan. Lee, do you want to kick off with a quick summary from your side?

[00:22] Lee (Polaris): yeah thanks. so over the last three weeks we've had repeated latency spikes and downstream 5xxs. our ops page shows memory pressure on the inference nodes and then the token latency climbs 2-3x, sometimes timeouts. we suspect the kv layer is evicting a large fraction of prefix keys during bursts. it's not constant, it kinda — it comes in waves.

[00:45] Samira (Polaris): to add, our workload is conversational with a lot of long-context sessions; many of the prefixes are re-used across sessions but not always the exact same order. we also recently enabled a more aggressive prefetch to try to reduce tail latency but that seemed to increase memory churn.

[01:05] Maya (Redwood): right.i think there are two interacting factors: hot-prefix churn and the prefetch policy filling hot slab spaces too eagerly, causing eviction cascades. we've seen similar in other customers where prefetch heuristics assume stable prefix affinity but the real distribution is multimodal.

[01:32] Ethan (Polaris): one thing we noticed — when we push larger batches during business hours, the KV spillback to disk increases and latencies go up. is that because the kv shard is doing synchronous spill? it's a little fuzzy in our telemetry.

[01:50] Ibrahim (Redwood Support): quick note, our runtime can spill to local NVMe and also optionally to a network tier for very large contexts. from the traces we saw you had both NVMe writes and paging events. sometimes the write amplification creates backpressure.

[02:12] Lee (Polaris): when you say "spill to network tier" do you mean S3-like object store? we can't allow unencrypted outbound traffic from our VPC.

[02:26] Maya (Redwood): good callout. for Private deployments we can configure spill to stay on-prem (local mounted volumes) and use your KMS; Redwood doesn't require outbound egress for spill if you're in VPC mode. seems like your config may have been toggled to enabled network spill during the stress tests.

[02:45] Talia (Polaris): can you walk through the eviction signature we should look for? what metrics to surface? CPU, mem, kv hits?

[03:02] Maya (Redwood): yes. primary signals: kv_eviction_rate (per-shard), kv_prefetch_fill_pct, kv_hot_prefix_count, kernel_vm_writeback/sec (if NVMe), and per-request kv_hit_latency histogram. correlate that with scheduler queue length and gpu-ready-latency. in practice the spike pattern is: prefetch increases, hot slab fill >80%, eviction rate jumps, prefix eviction causes next requests to miss and prefetch again - cycle.

[03:38] Samira (Polaris): is there a recommended safe prefetch threshold? we bumped from 64 to 128 tokens lookahead.

[03:48] Maya (Redwood): thresholds are workload dependent. for high prefix reuse you can push lookahead because prefetch reuse amortizes fill cost. for multimodal sessions with prefix churn, a smaller lookahead often reduces churn. we also recommend adaptive prefetch: start low, and for prefixes with >x reuse in last y minutes, increase.

[04:12] Jordan (Redwood): we're going to propose two parallel mitigations: short-term config changes to avoid runaway evictions, and a medium-term change to routing + routed batching to isolate hot prefixes and reduce cross-prefix thrash.

[04:28] Ethan (Polaris): routed batching? can you explain that more? sounds like more complexity.

[04:36] Maya (Redwood): sure — routed batching means grouping requests by prefix affinity into dedicated micro-pools. they'd have smaller, pinned KV residency so hot prefixes don't evict each other across the global pool. think of it as soft partitioning without provisioning full dedicated GPUs. it buys isolation and predictable tail latency.

[04:58] Lee (Polaris): are there cost implications? we want to avoid exploding costs if we need multiple pools.

[05:06] Maya (Redwood): yes there is a small cost premium because you reduce sharing, but you can autotune pool sizes. also combined with prefix-aware cache sizing and quantization (int8 for larger context models) you can often keep cost modest while stabilizing latency.

[05:28] Samira (Polaris): you mentioned quantization, our larger model variants are int8-ready but we're concerned about quality regression for long-context tasks. any guidance?

[05:40] Ibrahim (Redwood Support): we run evals on representative prompt sets; for many retrieval-augmented long-context tasks, int8 at the token-generation path has negligible impact if you keep KV storage lossless and only quantize compute matrices. but you should do prompt-level QA across your critical flows.

[06:05] Ethan (Polaris): during the last outage we saw long GC pauses at the OS level. could that be the NVMe writeback interacting with the container runtime?

[06:16] Maya (Redwood): yes, heavy writeback can cause pauses. recommended: async spill + bounded writeback threads and backpressure signals exposed as kv_writeback_pending. tune kernel dirty_ratio for the node and ensure the NVMe mount options avoid fsync-on-close.

[06:40] Samira (Polaris): what about prefix reuse heuristics — our sessions often stitch user messages and external tool outputs in different order, so prefix identity is fuzzy.

[06:52] Maya (Redwood): we support a prefix fingerprinting strategy — stable hashing over semantic chunks rather than raw token alignment. it reduces false misses when the order varies but the content overlaps. there is a tradeoff: coarser fingerprints increase chance of collisions; we expose a collision monitor.

[07:12] Jordan (Redwood): we're going to ask you to share concrete traces. ideally: a 30-minute window that includes a spike, full kv metrics, kernel/disk metrics, and the request sample with prefix ids. Samira/Ethan will that be possible?

[07:28] Samira (Polaris): yes we can pull from staging; we just need to sanitize user PII.

[07:34] Talia (Polaris): timeline wise we're evaluating for a Dedicated reserved pool next quarter — this triage is critical for sizing.

[07:46] Maya (Redwood): understood. sizing recommendations: if hot prefix fraction > 20% of requests, we often recommend a small hot-pool with pinned residency sized to 2-3x the hot working set. combined with increasing global eviction soft limits and adaptive prefetch this tends to reduce spill events.

[08:12] Ethan (Polaris): is there an automated way to detect a runaway eviction early? alerts we can add?

[08:19] Maya (Redwood): add an alert on kv_eviction_rate_rate_of_change > threshold, plus kv_prefetch_fill_pct > 85% for more than 30s, and a composite alert combining scheduler_queue_depth and kv_miss_ratio. we can share suggested prometheus alert expressions.

[08:46] Lee (Polaris): one question on telemetry and privacy: our legal team wants only aggregated telemetry off-box. we can't stream raw request payloads. how do you handle that for analysis?

[08:58] Jordan (Redwood): we can operate with hashed/fingerprinted prefixes and up-to N sample ids. for deep analysis we can work under an NDA and use a short-lived, scoped access token. we won't take raw PII without your permission.

[09:14] Samira (Polaris): let's talk about a reproducible replay. we have a kinesis-style event stream. can Redwood provide a replay harness or do you want us to run one and hand you traces?

[09:26] Maya (Redwood): we have a replay harness that's preferred because it preserves kv-access ordering and timing. easiest is you export a 30-60 minute trace with pointerized requests (no PII), we replay against a staging cluster instrumented with our tracing. we'll then run a diff of kv-residency and eviction events.

[09:48] Ethan (Polaris): ok we'll anonymize and upload. how long until you can analyze once we hand that over?

[09:54] Maya (Redwood): typical turnaround is 48-72 hours for an initial root-cause report. for a deeper optimization patch we may need 1-2 sprints.

[10:05] Talia (Polaris): can we simulate the failing pattern ourselves? which knobs give most deterministic repro?

[10:13] Maya (Redwood): two knobs: prefetch_lookahead and prefetch_budget_per_prefix. set lookahead high and budget low to force thrash, then run mixed session types. also increase request burst factor to simulate real traffic spikes. those will make eviction cycles appear quickly.

[10:32] Samira (Polaris): earlier you mentioned "softer eviction" — what exactly is that?

[10:38] Maya (Redwood): softer eviction is moving from immediate LRU eviction to a two-tiered approach: mark-for-evict + grace window where prefetch can rehydrate without full network/disk hit. effectively a short in-memory shadow for recently-evicted prefixes. reduces penalty for oscillating prefixes.

[11:02] Lee (Polaris): sounds expensive memory-wise. how to size the grace window?

[11:09] Maya (Redwood): small — typically 10-30 seconds depending on your session interarrival time. it's a configurable ring buffer and you only keep lightweight metadata (fingerprint + small kv header) until rehydration or final purge.

[11:28] Ethan (Polaris): is this feature available in the current runtime?

[11:33] Maya (Redwood): yes it's in our canary branch. we can propose a patch for your staging cluster as part of the PoC.

[11:42] Samira (Polaris): ok great. what are the risk factors for on-prem? we run in a locked-down VPC with strict host kernel versions.

[11:52] Ibrahim (Redwood Support): compatibility matrix: we support kernels >= 5.4 and certain NVMe drivers; we provide a packaged docker image that sets recommended sysctls. for older kernels we can run a compatibility shim but performance may vary. we'll capture exact variants in the checklist.

[12:14] Jordan (Redwood): I want to call out one incident signature we saw in your logs: a high kv_eviction_rate simultaneous with GC-like pause events and a spike in disk write latency. that combo usually points to synchronous spill + eviction cascade.

[12:33] Samira (Polaris): we did observe spikes in disk write latency. we'll share iostat and dstat for those windows.

[12:40] Maya (Redwood): one more practical mitigation: enable priority eviction lanes. system-level housekeeping and background prefetch threads can be separated so user-facing threads don't block on writeback. also recommended: tune io_uring queue depth for NVMe to avoid blocking user threads.

[13:05] Ethan (Polaris): regarding routed pools, how many pools should we start with? we have a few hundred prefixes that are medium frequency and a handful of really hot ones.

[13:16] Maya (Redwood): start with a single hot-pool for top N prefixes (N = hot_prefix_count where cumulative traffic > 30%). then a general pool for the rest. monitor cross-pool evictions and adjust. the runtime supports automatic hot prefix promotion if reuse crosses a threshold.

[13:42] Lee (Polaris): is the hot-pool pinned memory only or does it reserve GPU as well?

[13:49] Maya (Redwood): hot-pool pins KV residency and increases local memory reservation; it does not require separate GPUs though in high throughput cases we recommend co-locating with a small dedicated inference capacity.

[14:06] Samira (Polaris): we want concrete numbers to present to leadership for Dedicated sizing. can Redwood provide a calc sheet?

[14:13] Jordan (Redwood): yes we'll send a sizing worksheet based on working set, request qps, and prefix churn rate. that'll be part of the PoC package.

[14:26] Talia (Polaris): any gotchas on RBAC and audit logs when we move to private? our compliance team requires per-token audit log retention for 90 days.

[14:37] Jordan (Redwood): we support configurable retention windows and can push audit logs to your SIEM. for token-level retention you can keep pointer-level metadata off-box and redact payloads. we'll include the compliance matrix in the security FAQ.

[14:56] Maya (Redwood): quick technical aside about prefix fingerprinting collisions — we'll surface a collision_count metric and a sample collision log with hashed ids, so you can decide if fingerprint granularity needs adjusting.

[15:10] Samira (Polaris): perfect. about the replay harness — do you need the original request timing or can we accelerate time?

[15:18] Maya (Redwood): preserve relative timing and interarrival bursts; you can compress idle periods but keep the burst patterns intact. we'll document the export format in the replay guide.

[15:35] Ethan (Polaris): ok we'll start preparing traces. any sandbox creds or template we should use?

[15:41] Jordan (Redwood): I'll send a secure upload link and the replay template. also attaching the list of metrics we need.

[15:50] Samira (Polaris): on the long term what does Redwood recommend for preventing prefix thrash at scale?

[15:57] Maya (Redwood): multi-pronged: 1) prefix-aware routing + hot-pools; 2) adaptive prefetching with reuse counters; 3) softer eviction/grace windows; 4) telemetry driven autoscaling that reacts to kv_eviction_rate not just cpu/gpu; 5) targeted quantization to reduce memory footprint for non-critical models.

[16:24] Lee (Polaris): what's the expected timeline for PoC? we want results before end of quarter.

[16:30] Jordan (Redwood): if you can share traces this week, we can run staging replay and initial report in 48-72 hours, and then propose PoC configs within two weeks. that should meet your quarter request.

[16:45] Talia (Polaris): cool. let's confirm responsibilities and dates.

[17:00] Jordan (Redwood): recap: Redwood: run replay, send sizing calc, share security FAQ. Polaris: provide sanitized traces, node metrics, and confirm staging access window. target initial report by 2026-11-22 to 11-26.

[17:22] Samira (Polaris): one more smaller question — are there any existing toggles to prefer local NVMe spill over network spill in the config? we've seen an accidental switch before.

[17:30] Maya (Redwood): yes it's "spill_policy": "local-first" and then "spill_backoff_ms". we'll include recommended defaults for Private clusters.

[17:45] Ethan (Polaris): will the replay capture exact KV key ids so you can reconstruct hot prefixes, or do we need to map them?

[17:53] Maya (Redwood): fingerprints are fine. we only need stable hashed ids so we can compute reuse. avoid sharing raw keys.

[18:05] Lee (Polaris): thanks this was helpful. any blockers on your side?

[18:10] Jordan (Redwood): none. we'll get the templates and secure link after the call.

[18:18] Talia (Polaris): ok wrapping up. thanks everyone.

[18:25] Jordan (Redwood): thanks all — we'll follow up.

(Notes: transcript contains typical ASR artifacts — names sometimes mis-typed, timestamps are approximate. Full recording stored in Polaris shared drive per access instructions.)
